newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 13.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
FINANCIAL TIMES
UK GROWTH GAINS MOMENTUM

Figures released Wednesday show that growth in the UK gained momentum in January as unemployment fell to its lowest level for over six years and earnings increased at the fastest rate since February 1993. Separately, the quarterly inflation report from the Bank of England warned that the government would miss its target of 2.5 per cent in two years if interest rates remained at current levels. Chancellor Kenneth Clarke rejected calls from the Bank for a modest rise in interest rates.
UNILEVER CHIEF SLATED BY REDWOOD OVER EMU

John Redwood, a leading Conservative Euroskeptic MP, has criticised the chairman of the Anglo-Dutch group Unilever for indicating that the group might reconsider future investments in the UK if the government withdrew from discussions with Europe over preparations for monetary union. Redwood accused Niall FitzGerald, chairman of Unilever's UK arm, of playing politics at the shareholders' expense, and suggested that shareholders should confront FitzGerald over the issue.
LABOUR'S WINDFALL TAX WOULD HIT "WIDE RANGE OF COMPANIES'

Legal opinion provided for the Labour party has rejected claims that the party's proposed "windfall tax' on privatised utilities could be challenged in the European court. The advice, a joint opinion from Michael Beloff QC and Rabinder Singh, says the proposed levy would face no legal obstacles because it would apply to "a large and diverse number of sectors of the economy'. The revelation of the scope of the planned tax has been taken as an indication that the levy will hit companies ranging from British Telecom, British Gas and BAA, the airports operator.
TELECOMS CHIEF REBUFFS U.S. ATTACKS ON UK RULES

Don Cruickshank, the regulator of the UK telecommunications industry, has told an audience in the U.S. that the UK's telecoms policy is equal to -- if not better than -- any in the world. The comments come as U.S. and other foreign telecoms operators have criticised Britain's regulatory regime as they seek easier access to the UK market. Cruickshank claimed that U.S. regulatory methods were neither necessarily relevant to the UK, nor the most appropriate for markets outside the U.S.
LABOUR WOULD INVEST IN CLEAN COAL RESEARCH

A coal industry conference has heard that a future Labour government would invest in research into clean coal, and would review new consents for gas-fired power stations. Paddy Tipping, the Labour leader of the parliamentary minerals group, told the conference that coal was "in our tradition and in our blood', and also said a Labour government would amend the non-fossil fuel levy to include clean coal technology and solar power.
GROWTH IN MUSIC SALES DEFIES STANDSTILL IN GLOBAL MARKET

Figures released by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI), the body representing UK record companies, reveal that sales of albums and singles continued to grow in the UK in 1996 despite the global music market remaining virtually static. The BPI estimates that retail sales reached 1.08 billion stg last year, a rise of 6 per cent on 1995. Part of the growth has been attributed to the success of new acts such as the Spice Girls, Dodgy, and Ocean Colour Scene.
ITT MAY SELL ASSETS WORTH $2 BILLION

Hotel and casino company ITT, which is defending itself against a $6.5 billion (3.9 billion stg) hostile takeover bid from Hilton Hotels, has said it is reviewing various options to increase the value of the company including the disposal of non- core assets. A sale of non-core assets, which include a 50 per cent stake in New York's Madison Square Gardens and a five per cent stake in French group Alcatel Alsthom, could realise up to $2 billion.
CLYDE'S FRANKLIN OFFERED GULF JOB

In the latest twist in the 494 million stg hostile takeover bid by Gulf Canada Resources for UK oil independent Clyde Petroleum, Gulf has offered a job to Roy Franklin, chairman of Clyde, in the event of the takeover going ahead. Franklin responded by emphasising that his mind is solely on keeping Clyde independent. With the bid deadline due next Tuesday, both sides have launched new assaults on shareholders.
POLYGRAM SEES RETURN TO GROWTH

Dutch entertainment group PolyGram has forecast a return to growth in 1997 following two years of static profits. Shares in the group rose by Fl5.20 to Fl88.50 on Wednesday following the announcement of a slight fall in pre-tax profits for 1996, which come in the same week that the group received 14 Oscar nominations for its 1996 films. Despite this success, president Alain Levy also predicted another year of losses for the film division. PolyGram, the world's biggest music group, said it was confident that conditions in the global music market would improve after a "temporary lull' last year.
NATIONWIDE ACTS TO LURE CUSTOMERS FROM WOOLWICH

The Nationwide building society, one of the UK's biggest mutual societies, has signalled the start of what is expected to be a drive by the mutuals to attract business from rivals converting to banks. The Nationwide publicised the fact that its savings rates were consistently higher than those of the Woolwich, the society whose members voted on Wednesday to support plans to convert to a bank and float on the stock exchange.
